title: Congruences together: when two remainder conditions agree
attribution: RecallWeave contributors. Original questions, explanations, numerical examples and presentation. Mathematical background: MIT OpenCourseWare, Abhinav Kumar, 18.781 Theory of Numbers, Spring 2012, Lecture 5, Linear Congruences and the Chinese Remainder Theorem (https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-781-theory-of-numbers-spring-2012/7b36e2ada32c5ed0638783d4e66af60c_MIT18_781S12_lec5.pdf). No source exercise, passage or figure is reproduced.

items.prompt: Which number is the canonical remainder of −14 modulo 5? A canonical remainder r satisfies 0 ≤ r < 5.
items.explanation: The identity −14 = (−3) × 5 + 1 has remainder 1 in the required range. The negative remainder −4 also differs from −14 by a multiple of 5, but is not the canonical representative. Neither 4 nor 0 is congruent to −14 modulo 5.
items.transfer: Find the canonical remainder of −23 modulo 6. Verify it by writing −23 = 6q + r.

items.prompt: Which list contains only integers congruent to 3 modulo 7?
items.explanation: Subtracting 3 from −11, 3 and 17 gives −14, 0 and 14, each divisible by 7. A congruence describes infinitely many integers, including negative ones; it is not an equation that forces x = 3.
items.transfer: Write three other members of this residue class, including a negative integer, and check their differences from 3.

items.prompt: What restriction does x ≡ 4 (mod 1) impose on an integer x?
options: x must equal 4.
x must be positive.
x must be a multiple of 4.
It imposes no restriction.
items.explanation: Every integer difference x − 4 is divisible by 1. The sole canonical residue modulo 1 is zero, so normalizing the written residue 4 gives 0. Modulus 1 is valid and does not discard any integer candidate.
items.transfer: Combine x ≡ 4 (mod 1) with x ≡ 3 (mod 8). Give the least nonnegative solution and the period.

items.prompt: Which integer is the multiplicative inverse of 7 modulo 11?
items.explanation: 7 × 8 = 56 = 5 × 11 + 1, so 8 is an inverse. The other products have remainders 6, 5 and 10. An inverse is a multiplicative identity witness modulo the modulus, not an ordinary fraction.
items.transfer: Use the inverse to solve 7k ≡ 2 (mod 11), and check your k in the original congruence.

items.prompt: Does 6 have a multiplicative inverse modulo 9?
options: Yes: the inverse is 6.
Yes: the inverse is 3.
No: every 6k is divisible by 3.
No: inverses require a prime input.
items.explanation: If 6k were congruent to 1 modulo 9, then 6k − 1 would be divisible by 9 and hence by 3. But 6k is divisible by 3 and 1 is not. The obstruction is gcd(6, 9) = 3, not whether the input is prime.
items.transfer: Explain why 8 does have an inverse modulo 15 although both numbers are composite. Find one witness.

items.prompt: For x ≡ 2 (mod 6) and x ≡ 5 (mod 9), which compatibility check is correct?
options: gcd 3 divides difference 3, so a solution exists.
gcd 3 differs from 1, so no solution exists.
Product 54 divides difference 3, so a solution exists.
Residues 2 and 5 differ, so no solution exists.
items.explanation: The gcd is 3 and the normalized residue difference is 5 − 2 = 3. Divisibility by the gcd is the condition. Shared factors do not automatically cause a contradiction; here 14 leaves remainders 2 and 5. Coprime moduli guarantee compatibility for every residue pair, but they are not necessary for this particular pair.
items.transfer: Change only the second residue so the system becomes incompatible. State the new difference and its remainder modulo the gcd.

items.prompt: Why is there no integer satisfying x ≡ 1 (mod 4) and x ≡ 2 (mod 6)?
options: The two moduli are different.
The product of the moduli is too large.
Every nonzero pair of residues is incompatible.
The first condition requires odd x; the second requires even x.
items.explanation: The first class consists of odd integers and the second of even integers. Equivalently, gcd(4, 6) = 2 does not divide the difference 2 − 1 = 1. This is an exact contradiction, not a failed search within a small displayed range.
items.transfer: Replace the second residue with an odd one and determine whether the two constraints become compatible.

items.prompt: How do x ≡ 6 (mod 7) and x ≡ −1 (mod 7) combine?
options: They contradict because the written residues differ.
They are the same class, x ≡ 6 (mod 7).
They give the single integer x = 6.
They repeat only every 49 integers.
items.explanation: −1 normalizes to 6 modulo 7. Both conditions select the same integers. Repeating an identical condition adds no restriction and does not multiply its period. The complete class is 6 + 7k for integer k.
items.transfer: Give two differently written residues modulo 9 that describe the same class, then two that describe incompatible classes.

items.prompt: What is the least nonnegative integer satisfying x ≡ 3 (mod 4) and x ≡ 2 (mod 5)?
items.explanation: The integers 3, 7, 11, 15, 19 are the first representatives of the first class below 20. Only 7 has remainder 2 modulo 5. Check both equations: 7 = 1 × 4 + 3 and 7 = 1 × 5 + 2. The integer 17 meets the second condition but not the first.
items.transfer: Find the next positive solution and one negative solution. Verify both remainders using nonnegative canonical residues.

items.prompt: For x = 2 + 6k to also satisfy x ≡ 5 (mod 9), divide 6k ≡ 3 (mod 9) by gcd 3. The reduced equation is 2k ≡ 1 (mod 3). Which k is its canonical solution?
items.explanation: Modulo 3, the inverse of 2 is 2 because 2 × 2 = 4 ≡ 1. Thus k ≡ 2, producing x = 2 + 6 × 2 = 14. Dividing the coefficient, target and modulus by their common gcd preserves the appropriate solution class for k; dividing only the target would not.
items.transfer: Starting from the identity (−1) × 6 + 1 × 9 = 3, explain how the coefficient −1 becomes the inverse 2 of 6/3 modulo 9/3.

items.prompt: For x ≡ 5 (mod 12) and x ≡ 1 (mod 4), the reduced second modulus is 4/gcd(12, 4) = 1. What does this mean?
options: The second condition adds no restriction; x = 5 + 12k.
The input is invalid because a reduced modulus is 1.
The system has no solution because inverse modulo 1 is missing.
The period becomes 48 because both moduli must be multiplied.
items.explanation: Every integer 5 + 12k has remainder 1 modulo 4. The canonical multiplier modulo 1 is zero, so no inverse operation is needed. The least nonnegative solution is 5 and the period remains 12. The explorer labels this case directly rather than inventing an ordinary inverse modulo 1.
items.transfer: Reverse the order of the two congruences and show that the least nonnegative solution and period are unchanged.

items.prompt: For the solution x ≡ 7 (mod 20), which description gives every integer solution?
options: Only x = 7.
x = 7 + 20k for any integer k.
x = 7k for any integer k.
x = 20 + 7k for any integer k.
items.explanation: The integer parameter k may be positive, zero or negative. For example, k = −1, 0, 1 gives −13, 7 and 27. A least nonnegative representative names a whole class; it is not the only solution and is not a promise about a physical schedule.
items.transfer: If you want only solutions in the integer interval [0, 100], list them and explain why restricting the interval is a separate condition.

items.prompt: Compatible conditions with moduli 6 and 9 repeat together after what least positive period?
items.explanation: A difference between common solutions must be divisible by both moduli, so it must be a multiple of lcm(6, 9) = 6 × 9 / 3 = 18. The product 54 repeats but is not least; gcd 3 does not preserve either remainder in general. For the residues 2 and 5, the class is 14 + 18k.
items.transfer: Give the least period for compatible constraints with moduli 8 and 12. Explain why their product is unnecessarily large.

items.prompt: An inspector displays 24 consecutive integers and none matches both residue conditions. What can you conclude from that display alone?
options: The whole system is incompatible.
The least solution must be negative.
The period must be less than 24.
That particular 24-integer window contains no solution.
items.explanation: A compatible system may have a period much larger than the displayed window and its first solution may lie elsewhere. The exact gcd/difference test establishes compatibility; a bounded display only illustrates its chosen integers. For example, x ≡ 40 (mod 101) with a redundant modulus-1 condition has no solution among 0 through 23.
items.transfer: Choose a compatible system whose first solution lies beyond 23. Explain how the exact result and the bounded display can agree.
